headline: High-risk default write/egress overlap and workflow chaining can leak data or cascade errors; prompt-injection risk is lower but present via shared files/stdin.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write files and use stdin/stdout, so content from kestra can be passed into ms-swift as trusted text or config. Kestra’s declarative workflows and ms-swift’s CLI/Python workflow make file-mediated instruction smuggling plausible. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred rather than proven.
conditions: IF kestra writes workflow text or logs into a file that ms-swift later parses as instructions or config
IF the operator pipes stdout from one agent directly into the other without sanitization
mitigations: Use separate directories for each agent's files
Insert a manual review step before piping outputs between agents
Rename and segregate workflow/config files from free-form text
Disable stdin piping between agents unless explicitly needed
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to files passed between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Kestra has broad network egress and touches logs, inputs, artifacts, database data, cloud storage data, messages, and notifications; ms-swift handles datasets, checkpoints, outputs, and secrets like hub_token/sdk-token. If they share a workspace or pass files, sensitive data can flow from one into the other and then out via Kestra’s APIs or ms-swift’s model/hub interfaces. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default operator setups.
conditions: IF both agents are run on the same host with overlapping file access
IF kestra workflows ingest files that contain ms-swift checkpoints, adapters, or tokens
IF ms-swift is configured to upload datasets or outputs through its listed APIs
mitigations: Place each agent in a separate filesystem namespace
Keep secrets out of shared directories and logs
Review any file handoff before execution
Restrict ms-swift to non-sensitive datasets
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent egress allowlists and DLP scanning

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell, spawn subprocesses, read and write the filesystem, and use network egress. Kestra also requests root and docker.sock, while ms-swift can install packages. On a shared host, concurrent writes and environment changes can collide, and Kestra’s elevated privileges make the conflict blast radius larger than a simple local race.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same writable directory
IF kestra runs with root or docker.sock access while ms-swift installs packages or rewrites configs
IF the orchestrator does not serialize filesystem mutations
mitigations: Assign disjoint working directories
Run only one writer at a time
Avoid granting kestra root or docker.sock unless required
Pin ms-swift package versions before execution
requires-engineering: add file locks around shared mutable resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: Kestra produces workflow outputs, logs, artifacts, and notifications that ms-swift can consume as datasets, configuration, or evaluation inputs. Because ms-swift can act on CLI/Python inputs without a documented verification gate, a bad Kestra output can propagate into downstream model runs or reports. The pairwise chain is therefore a default-path cascade, not just a theoretical one.
conditions: IF ms-swift consumes Kestra-generated artifacts, logs, or notifications as training/eval input
IF no human verification step exists between Kestra output and ms-swift execution
mitigations: Add a manual approval step between agents
Validate Kestra outputs before handing them to ms-swift
Use schema checks on files exchanged between agents
Limit ms-swift to read-only evaluation runs for first pass
requires-engineering: implement typed contracts for inter-agent handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: Kestra explicitly touches database data, cloud storage data, messages, and notifications, while ms-swift handles datasets, checkpoints, training outputs, and secrets. The profiles do not state residency or retention controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible if regulated data is routed through both. Because no specific jurisdiction or certification gap is documented, this stays medium rather than high.
conditions: IF regulated data such as customer messages or database records is routed through both agents
IF retention or deletion policies differ between Kestra artifacts and ms-swift outputs
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workflows
Document retention for each agent's outputs
Separate sensitive and non-sensitive pipelines
Review where secrets are stored and logged
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls
